ety.text: Borrowed from Sanskrit कर्म (kárma), nom.sg. of कर्मन् (kárman, “act, action, performance”); first attested in English in 1785 in a translation of the Bhagavad Gita by Charles Wilkins.

senses.d: The sum total of a person's actions, which determine the person's next incarnation in samsara, the cycle of death and rebirth.
ex: ‘We are all part of a circle of karma. We will be rewarded for the good deeds of our forefathers, and pay the price for their sins.’

senses.d: A force or law of nature which causes one to reap what one sows; destiny; fate.
A distinctive feeling, aura, or atmosphere.
ex: That means everything from lighting to the vibes, the karma of the room.
On the way to Lancaster, which was about an hour and a half from Philly, John felt the karma.

senses.d: A score assigned to a user or post on some discussion forums, indicating popularity or perceived value.

grp.label: the total effect of a person’s actions and conduct during the successive phases of his existence

ety.text: Sanskrit कर्मन् (karman)bor. Portuguese carma Borrowed from Sanskrit कर्मन् (karman).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin clīma, from Ancient Greek κλῐ́μᾰ (klĭ́mă, “region, zone”), from κλῐ́νω (klĭ́nō, “to slope, incline”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean”).
Borrowed from Japanese 空(から)手(て) (karate), from 唐(から)手(て) (karate), an orthographic borrowing from Okinawan 唐手(とーでぃー) (tōdī, “Chinese hand”).

senses.d: An Okinawan martial art involving primarily punching and kicking, but additionally, advanced throws, arm bars, grappling and all means of fighting.
ex: Prior to the coronavirus pandemic, Wall taught karate at a local nursing home.

senses.d: To attack (somebody or something) with karate or similar techniques.
